page: Microsoft Azure D1pls_v7 is an entry-level virtual machine instance within the general-purpose Dplsv7 series, operating on the 64-bit ARM (arm64) architecture. Managed under Microsoft Hyper-V virtualization, the instance is provisioned with 1 dedicated virtual CPU core and 2.0 GB of system memory, yielding a 1:2 vCPU-to-memory ratio. The configuration includes no discrete GPUs.

The D1pls_v7 instance does not include bundled local disk storage, necessitating the attachment of remote block volumes for the operating system and persistent data. The instance is capable of attaching Premium Storage tiers. In addition, there are zero complimentary public IPv4 addresses included with the hardware profile, requiring external network routing configurations or dedicated IP allocation for ingress connectivity.

With a dedicated arm64 compute core and a small memory envelope, the instance provides an economical entry point for lightweight services without shared-core CPU contention. The primary constraint is the 2.0 GB memory capacity, which precludes high concurrency or memory-intensive database software. It is suited for small-scale microservices, lightweight web servers, background workers, and CI/CD agent tasks.
description: Microsoft Azure D1pls_v7 is an entry-level ARM-based virtual machine configured with 1 dedicated arm64 vCPU and 2.0 GB of RAM. Positioned within the general-purpose Dplsv7 series as a low-memory option, it maintains a 1:2 vCPU-to-memory ratio under Microsoft Hyper-V virtualization. The instance includes no onboard GPU hardware and does not bundle local disk storage, requiring the use of remote persistent storage volumes, with support for Azure Premium Storage. Public network connectivity requires configured external IP resources, as zero complimentary public IPv4 addresses are included. Without integrated local disks, persistent I/O performance relies on network-attached disks. The lean hardware allocation offers a cost-conscious compute baseline with low operational overhead, though the 2.0 GB RAM boundary restricts heavy multi-threaded execution or large datasets. It is technically appropriate for lightweight microservices, background automation tasks, small reverse proxies, CI/CD runners, and development or testing environments.
